page_contents_html:
Chronic diarrhoea investigation

Assess persistent loose stool systematically in primary care, looking for cancer, inflammation, infection, medication effects and malabsorption before referral.

Local update: include HIV serology in the initial GP blood panel

HIV testing should be completed in primary care alongside the other first-line blood tests rather than deferred to secondary assessment. Discuss the test and obtain consent in the usual way.

Use faecal calprotectin selectively after qFIT when inflammatory bowel disease remains a realistic differential; it is not a screening test for every patient with diarrhoea.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
History and examination

  • Duration, stool frequency and form, nocturnal symptoms, urgency, incontinence, blood or mucus
  • Weight loss, fever, abdominal pain, recent antibiotics, travel and infection exposure
  • Family history of colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease
  • Diet, alcohol, previous bowel or gallbladder surgery, pancreatitis and radiotherapy
  • Review medicines that can cause diarrhoea, including laxatives, metformin, PPIs, NSAIDs, SSRIs and magnesium-containing products

Examine for dehydration, weight loss, anaemia, abdominal mass, perianal disease and faecal impaction/overflow. Perform rectal examination where clinically indicated.

Initial GP investigations

Blood tests:

  • FBC
  • CRP
  • TFT
  • Coeliac serology: tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA
  • HIV serology

Stool tests:

  • qFIT in line with the current lower gastrointestinal symptoms pathway
  • Stool culture and other infection testing when clinically indicated
  • Ova, cysts and parasites when exposure or travel history makes this relevant
  • Faecal calprotectin only when qFIT is negative, symptoms persist and inflammatory bowel disease remains a realistic differential

If coeliac serology is positive, refer for gastroenterology assessment and confirmation. Advise the patient to continue eating gluten until assessment is complete.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
• Treat dehydration and correct clinically important nutritional or electrolyte disturbance.
  • Stop or adjust a possible causative medicine where safe, then review the response.
  • Treat an identified infective or other cause according to the relevant pathway.
  • Use the colorectal pathway when cancer is suspected and the gastroenterology pathway when inflammatory bowel disease is suspected.
  • When assessment is satisfactory and symptoms fit IBS-D, provide IBS management and consider dietetic input rather than routinely requesting further tests.

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Urgent assessment

Use the current suspected-cancer or acute pathway for rectal bleeding, unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia, abdominal or rectal mass, significant unintentional weight loss, a concerning qFIT result, severe dehydration or acute systemic illness.

Refer to gastroenterology

  • Suspected inflammatory bowel disease
  • Positive coeliac serology
  • Persistent chronic diarrhoea with diagnostic uncertainty after the initial assessment
  • Evidence of malabsorption, pancreatic disease or another condition requiring specialist investigation
  • A clearly raised faecal calprotectin, or a persistently borderline result with compatible symptoms, using current local laboratory guidance

Include symptom duration and pattern, weight trend, medication review, relevant examination, qFIT, faecal calprotectin if indicated, stool microbiology and all blood results including HIV serology.

Consider dietetics

For patients aged under 40 with satisfactory assessment and IBS-D symptoms, consider gastroenterology dietetic input in line with the current local pathway.

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Specialist medical referral is usually unnecessary when:

  • A reversible medicine or dietary cause has been identified and symptoms settle after intervention
  • Symptoms meet IBS-D criteria, there are no alarm features, initial investigations are satisfactory and symptoms can be managed in primary care or with dietetic support
  • There is a short-lived infective illness that is resolving and does not require specialist care

Do not request faecal calprotectin repeatedly without a clinical question or use it in place of qFIT when colorectal cancer is a concern.

accordion_sections.heading: Further investigation usually arranged or directed by secondary care
accordion_sections.html:
• Malabsorption: iron, B12, folate, calcium, albumin and faecal elastase as indicated
  • Immunodeficiency: immunoglobulins; confirm that primary-care HIV testing has been completed
  • Microscopic colitis: colonoscopy with biopsies
  • Inflammatory bowel disease: endoscopic assessment guided by symptoms and faecal calprotectin
  • Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency: faecal elastase and pancreatic imaging when indicated
  • Bile acid diarrhoea: specialist testing or treatment according to local practice
  • Lactose intolerance or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth: breath testing or specialist-directed treatment where appropriate

notes_for_editor: Local-request update: HIV serology has been moved into the initial primary-care blood panel; secondary care should confirm it has already been completed.
Faecal calprotectin is framed as a selective IBD-versus-IBS test after qFIT, not a routine screen for every patient with diarrhoea.
Confirm current D&G laboratory faecal calprotectin thresholds, local stool microbiology requesting details and exact referral routes before publication.
Medication examples are prompts for clinical review rather than an exhaustive list.
